items.title: Why Your Services Randomly Throw 502 Bad Gateway Behind AWS ALB (And the 3-Line Fix)
items.summary: If your microservices behind an AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB) are intermittently throwing 502 Bad Gateway errors—especially during low-traffic valleys, background cron runs, or right after a quiet spell—stop debugging your memory limits. Your server is not crashing, your CPU is not spiking, and your security groups are completely fine. You are hitting a microsecond TCP in-flight race condition. By default, an AWS ALB maintains idle backend TCP connections for 60 seconds. If your backend web framework (Node.js, Python Uvicorn, or Go) has a default keep-alive timeout of 50 or 60 seconds, your backend process will close the idle socket with a TCP FIN packet at the exact microsecond the ALB decides to forward a new client request down that same socket. The packets cross on the wire. The ALB receives a TCP RST (Connection Reset) on an in-flight request, gives up immediately, and dumps an HTTP 502 directly into your user's lap. items.summary: I wanted a clear victory for my language, Vow. I built a sandbox to stop AI agents from doing things they should not do. I tested it against 7 attack programs. The one that got through happened because Vow did not have a read-only file grant. There was no way to tell the program it could read a folder without also giving it permission to write. I fixed it. On November 12, 2026, I added a read-only file grant. I ran the test again. Vow blocked 7 of 7. TypeScript under Deno also blocked 7 of 7. A tie. I spent my time working to see my language win, but it only matched the performance of the established tool. There is a second part to the test. items.summary: Originally published at https://bestlatestapps.com/blog/how-to-generate-an-apns-jwt-provider-token-from-a-p8-key/. Token-based push authentication is simpler than certificates once it works. Getting it to work the first time, though, usually involves a 403 InvalidProviderToken with no further explanation. APNs JWT generator builds and signs a correct token from your .p8 key, Key ID and Team ID, decodes it, counts down to expiry, and gives you a curl command to test against APNs. An APNs provider token is a JWT: Header: {"alg": "ES256", "kid": " "} Claims: {"iss": " ", "iat": } Each part is base64url-encoded without padding, joined with a dot, and signed using ECDSA on the P-256 curve with SHA-256. The base64url signature becomes the third part. The page does the signing with the browser's Web Crypto API and shows the decoded header and claims next to the result. Key ID: in Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles → Keys, and in the file name AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8 (the page reads it from the name when it can). items.title: Contract Testing 101: How to Prevent Breaking API Changes in Node.js
items.summary: What Is Contract Testing? Contract testing is a software testing methodology that verifies whether two separate applications—typically a client service making requests and a server API delivering data—can safely communicate with each other. Instead of booting up both services simultaneously in a live environment to test their interactions, contract testing checks each service independently against an agreed-upon formal specification known as a contract. If either side makes a code change that violates this shared contract, the automated test suite immediately flags the incompatibility before deployment. In microservice architectures, an API (Application Programming Interface) acts as the bridge connecting disparate services. Contract testing ensures that the provider of the API continues delivering data in the exact structural format (JSON keys, data types, and status codes) expected by the consumer of the API. items.title: macOS 27 quietly renamed the screenshot location key
items.summary: I'm Bazi, and I make Pizazoo, a screenshot organizer for Mac, iPhone and iPad. Pizazoo doesn't take screenshots. On the Mac it organizes the ones you take with Shift-Command-3, 4 or 5 (or apps like CleanShot X, Shottr and Xnapper) by watching the folders they save to. So "where does macOS save screenshots?" is a question my app has to answer correctly, and in Settings the System Screenshots row has a Change Location… button that changes the answer. On macOS 27 that button stopped working. You picked a folder, the app wrote the setting, restarted SystemUIServer like it always had, and the next screenshot saved exactly where it did before. On a Mac where nothing had set the new key, that meant the Desktop. No error, no failed write. The setting simply had no effect. items.title: React useReducer --- Basic Notes:
items.summary: What it does: Takes the current state and an action, and returns a newState. (state, action) => newState Syntax: const[score, dispatch] = useReducer ( reducerfn, initialvalue); Main Parts: 1)​score (state): The current value/variable. ​ 2)dispatch: The function used to send an action. ​ 3)reducerFn: The function that decides how the state changes. ​ 4)initialValue: The starting value of the state. ​ 5)action: An object (like { type: "Increment" }) that tells what change to make. Example: const reducerFn = (state, action) => { switch (action.type) { case "Increment": return state + 1; case "Decrement": return state - 1; case "Reset": return 0; default: return state; } };

When a signal changes, the dependent computation can update directly. That model has always been attractive for interfaces with frequent, localized updates. items.summary: As of November 16, 2026, webatla counts 11,053,868 websites running React, 3.39% of the 325.8 million websites it tracks. The scan finds a version string on only about 4,500 of them. Any answer to how many websites use React depends on what a scanner can observe in a React site, and that is worth understanding if you write or maintain React code. The live number sits on webatla's React technology page. The history tables and the full framework comparison are in the React statistics article on the webatla blog. React renders in the browser and, in many setups, on the server as well. Either way the browser receives HTML plus JavaScript files, and React's client code takes over the page once they load. A CMS usually leaves fixed paths in the markup, and a web server often names itself in a response header. React leaves neither. Its presence has to be inferred from the JavaScript a site ships. webatla's React page is direct about what that means. It finds React where a site exposes it through recognizable build output or development artifacts. A bundle compiled tightly enough leaves no reliable trace, and such sites stay out of the file. items.title: 26 of our files use framer-motion's m, one uses motion, and that one renders on every public page
items.summary: framer-motion has a well known tax and a well known way of avoiding it. If you import motion you get the whole animation engine, because motion.div has to support every feature anyone might pass it. If you import m instead, you get a component with no features at all, and you choose what to load by wrapping a subtree in LazyMotion: import { LazyMotion, domAnimation, m } from 'framer-motion' The library ships its own size fixtures, so the difference is not a matter of opinion. From framer-motion@12.40.0 in our own node_modules: fixture raw gzipped size-rollup-dom-animation-m.js (m plus domAnimation) 7,341 3,150 size-rollup-dom-animation.js 37,331 13,938 size-rollup-dom-max.js 84,742 27,488 size-rollup-motion.js (plain motion) 123,572 39,455 We knew all of this. I went and counted what we actually do. Across app/, components/ and hooks/, 32 files import from framer-motion: 26 import m 9 render a LazyMotion provider, 8 of them with domAnimation 1 uses domMax 7 use AnimatePresence, 5 use MotionConfig 1 imports motion Twenty-six to one. items.title: MCP Unlocked: Building a Claude‑Ready AI Agent Server with CDK and Node.js
items.summary: AI agents keep tripping over context limits because they don’t speak the Model Context Protocol (MCP). By the end of this guide you’ll have a real, deployable server that talks MCP‑fluently to Claude, so your assistant can call tools without a single manual hack. MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. Think of it as a common language that lets a large language model (LLM) like Claude ask a downstream service to run a tool and receive a structured answer. Without MCP the model has to “explain” the tool call in plain text, and the surrounding code has to parse that text back into a request – a fragile round‑trip that often exceeds the model’s token budget. In plain English: MCP is a tiny contract (JSON schema + HTTP semantics) that removes guesswork. The model says “run this tool with these arguments”, the server replies with a clean JSON payload, and the conversation can continue without re‑sending the whole prompt. Why does this matter? Predictable token usage – The model only needs to embed the MCP request once, instead of repeating tool definitions. It was a straightforward calculation involving a few Double conversions and some basic arithmetic. Every clean build took noticeably longer than expected, and when I ran the compiler with type-checking timers enabled, that one line was the culprit. This experience sent me down a path I'd been avoiding for years: actually reading what swiftc produces between my source file and the binary. This article is the write-up I wish I'd had at the start. items.title: One command, four minutes, $3.73: what an AI security review found in OWASP NodeGoat
items.summary: My last two posts were about AI security scanners getting things wrong: one reported bugs in code it never read and one showed $0.00 for a cost nobody knew. Fair question after all that: what does a run look like when it works and how do you check it? So here's a real one. No edits, no cherry-picking. secfoo, the open-source (MIT) tool our team at RakFort builds, pointed at OWASP NodeGoat, with the same checks I used to catch those earlier bugs. uvx secfoo run --skill sast --skill secret-scanning \ --target https://github.com/OWASP/NodeGoat --fail-on high That's the whole setup. No config file. secfoo picks whichever coding agent you already have installed (this run used Claude Code), clones the repo, hands the agent a fixed security brief and collects a report in a fixed format. NodeGoat is a deliberately vulnerable Node.js/Express/MongoDB app that OWASP uses for training. That makes it a good test: its bugs are planted on purpose and documented, so you can check the scanner against a known answer. The run is from 14 November, using quick depth, with both skills running at the same time. Skill Critical High Medium Low Time Cost Static code analysis 0 6 5 1 4 min 12 s $2.34 Secret

items.title: Discord bot offline a week while systemd said active: a plugin timeout
items.summary: Discord is how I talk to my homelab's AI agents. It's basically the front door. From 30 September to 7 October 2026 that front door was shut, and everything I had watching it said it was fine. hermes-gateway (the agent's gateway, Hermes Agent) was active (running) my gateway watchdog was green the gateway's own state file said Discord was connected None of that was true for Discord. This is how a 10 second timeout did a week of damage. Around 02:02 on 30 September the Proxmox node that runs the agent rebooted. That node keeps all its guests on one 5400rpm hard disk, so every boot is an IO storm for a good 15 minutes. I wrote about that separately. The short version is that everything starting up is fighting over one slow spindle, so everything is slow. The gateway loads its chat platforms as plugins. Each plugin gets a time limit to import and register itself: plugins.load_timeout_seconds, which defaults to 10 seconds. On a calm boot that's loads. In the middle of the storm, the Discord plugin's import didn't make it. When I dug into it on 7 October, the logs were clear enough: The plugin timed out after 10 seconds. Its register_platform() call did come back, about 0.7 seconds late

items.title: Validating a High-Performance Cloud Object Store with Lightweight Formal Methods
items.summary: Abstract: We report on our experience validating S3 Express One Zone, a high-performance Amazon S3 storage class launched in November 2023. We focused on its distributed metadata index, which implements a hierarchical namespace using distributed transactions. We check strong consistency and durability under crashes, network delays, and timeouts. Building on our prior work on lightweight formal methods, we combined executable reference models with property-based testing and stateless model checking. Applying these techniques to a production distributed system required three new techniques: a white-box approach to checking serializability; compositional validation of the data and control planes; and long-running canaries that use reference models to check correctness across deployments. We extended Shuttle, our open-source stateless checker, to support a production async Rust runtime and failure injection, including cancelled operations and timeouts. items.title: Stop Using Exceptions for Control Flow: Railway-Oriented Programming in C#
items.summary: An expired coupon or insufficient credit is not a system crash—it is normal business behavior. Throwing exceptions for routine mistakes buries domain logic under nested if/else blocks, slows down execution, and forces callers to guess what might fail. Railway-Oriented Programming (ROP) models workflows as a two-track railway: Success Track: Data moves forward step by step through clean, linear functions. Failure Track: Any failed rule switches tracks and skips all remaining steps—with zero throw or try/catch blocks. Input ──► [ Validate ] ──► [ Get Coupon ] ──► [ Check Rules ] ──► [ Calculate ] ──► Success │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ (Failure Track) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────► Failure(Errors) Full Source Code: Explore the complete C# implementation, conditional workflows, and runnable console demo on GitHub at stevsharp/RailwayOrientedCSharp. Dishonest Signatures: A method returning Task promises a number every time while hiding four or five hidden exceptions inside. items.title: Satellites Now Outnumber the Visible Stars Above Most Towns
items.summary: Satellites now outnumber visible stars in the night sky above many towns and cities, according to a non-peer-reviewed analysis by engineering firm Accu Components. The researchers estimated that roughly 710 satellites pass over an average U.K. town at any given moment, with about 105 illuminated by sunlight and potentially visible to the naked eye. Space.com reports: Although the researchers specifically focused on the U.K., they say that such heavy satellite traffic flows above most of Europe, the U.S. and other mid-latitude regions, especially between 40 and 50 degrees north or south. "Most Starlink satellites orbit at around 53 degrees to the equator, so the satellites bunch up over the mid-latitudes. These worldwide figures are approximate, based on a global grid over a single day," Accu Components spokesperson told Space.com in an email. "Skies near the equator are the quietest, with around 490 satellites." Not all of those satellites are visible to the naked eye, the researchers said in a statement. items.summary: Welcome to our weekly log for the Supabase .NET SDK 🎉 Sorry for being a little late on this one. As usual, coming back from PTO is always intense. The SDK is currently at version v8.12.0 and v8.13.0 will most likely get published later today, with 18+ new supported features. Over the last three weeks, the feature coverage bumped significantly, from a starting 50% to 70% currently. My goal is to reach 100% by the end of the year, making sure the SDK exposes every feature available on our platform. It is ambitious, but I'm confident that we'll end up very close. The work on feature parity also shapes what will happen in the future v9. You'll find a migration guide for v9.0.0 in the repository which lists upcoming changes. I try to avoid breaking changes at the moment as I can't afford bumping a new major right now, so I have to make compromises here and there. items.title: GPU Watch – Monitor remote NVIDIA GPUs from your Mac menu bar over SSH
items.summary: I built a native macOS menu bar app to monitor NVIDIA GPUs across remote Linux servers. One problem I kept running into was how monitoring tools handle failures. If SSH goes down, that doesn't mean eight GPUs have failed. And if nvidia-smi stops responding, we shouldn't report its last known values as current. GPU Watch keeps SSH connectivity, GPU query results, and data freshness separate. Monitor multiple hosts over SSH No agent installed on remote servers Uses your existing SSH config and keys Tracks physical GPUs by UUID No backend, telemetry, or third-party dependencies Written in Swift/SwiftUI, open source under GPLv3 It's currently available as a source build for macOS. Built at SIAM.AI, and I'd appreciate feedback from anyone managing remote GPU servers. GitHub: https://github.com/siamaicorp/GPUWatch

The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion. Gallup's study is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children's Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries. A lot of the topline results won't surprise anyone living in today's constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. Three things that stood out were how the young respondents talked about AI, loneliness, and doomscrolling. items.title: Day 26: Numeric Semantics, Multiple Currencies and Units of Measure
items.summary: The chapters so far asked whether a value gets in, whether it gets across, and whether it gets recorded. This post asks a different question: what the value that got in actually stands for. The quantity, unit price, amount, discount rate and exchange rate on a document look almost identical in the TableSchema definition, each one a decimal number with a precision. The real difference lies in three places: how many decimal places to show, whether to round when the value is written, and who has the say over the number of places. Most systems hand these three to the table's DDL, the format strings on screen, and the Math.Round calls in the business logic, and each of the three gets changed on its own. To be maintainable, the three have to be governed by one mechanism. items.title: Rate Limiting in Vineforce Teams: Designing Dynamic API Policies on ASP.NET Core
items.summary: Overview Vineforce Teams is built on ASP.NET Zero, and it inherits ASP.NET Zero's dynamic rate limiting feature. Rate limiting policies are not hard-coded in Program.cs or appsettings.json. Administrators create them from the Administration > Rate Limiting screen, they are stored in the database, and they take effect at runtime without a restart or redeployment. This article explains how that feature works under the hood, how a request is matched to a policy, and how to design a policy set that protects the API without throttling legitimate users. It is written for developers, architects, and DevOps engineers who operate or extend Vineforce Teams, particularly in on-premise deployments. Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a time window, or how many it can have in flight at once. For a multi-tenant time-tracking platform it addresses four concrete risks: Credential attacks. Anonymous endpoints such as /api/TokenAuth/* are the first target for credential stuffing and password spraying. A per-IP limit makes large-scale guessing slow and noisy. Resource exhaustion. items.title: Best Buy Resumes Blu-ray Sales
items.summary: Best Buy has resumed selling Blu-ray movies directly through its website and physical stores after exiting the physical media business in 2023. The retailer currently offers a limited selection of 15 Blu-ray listings, including new releases like The Odyssey and Project Hail Mary and older titles like It's a Wonderful Life (1943), Saving Private Ryan (1998), and The Godfather (1972). Ars Technica reports: Overall, the sales of Blu-rays and DVDs in the US have been steadily declining, and annual consumer spending dropped 9.3 percent from 2024 to 2025, according to the Digital Entertainment Group (DEG). During this same time, however, consumer spending on 4K Blu-ray discs specifically increased 12 percent year over year, per DEG. "We're seeing a lot of evidence, including at the Criterion Mobile Closet, that more young people are thinking about physical media in a different way," Peter Becker, president of Criterion, which sells Blu-rays and DVDs online, told the Los Angeles Times in February. "In an age where so much is available to us on demand, it becomes increasingly important to us." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: 'Java4Shell' Flaw Exposes OpenJDK to RCE via Base64
items.summary: Longtime Slashdot reader HnT writes: Security researchers at Calif have disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a critical 9.2-rated memory-corruption bug in OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder. By sending a malformed string ending in a stray = character, attackers can trigger an out-of-bounds heap write to leak sensitive memory or achieve pre-auth remote code execution on major platforms like Jira, Jenkins, and Keycloak. Although Calif says the vulnerability is difficult to exploit, Oracle released a critical patch update Tuesday, and CISA urged organizations to update immediately. items.title: Cambridge Dictionary Names 'Human' Its 2026 Word of the Year
items.summary: Cambridge Dictionary has named "human" its 2026 Word of the Year, reflecting growing concerns about artificial intelligence and its impact on what it means to be human. "AI is changing how we talk about being human," said Colin McIntosh, the dictionary's lexicographer. "Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking have made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children." The Associated Press reports: The adjective derived from the Latin "humanus" and in use since the 1450s is defined by Cambridge as "having the qualities, faults and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals or machines." items.summary: Hi HN, we're Shane, Sam, and Abhi. Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073. It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races. Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself. At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans. There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack. items.title: A receipt that says "nothing was changed" has to be true
items.summary: Our Mac menu bar app has two buttons, Free Agent RAM and Stop Runaways. Each one runs a small Node.js script that finds agent processes eating memory or CPU, and stops them. When the script finishes, the app shows a receipt that lists what it did. If Node.js isn't installed, the script can't run. The app handles that: it shows "Couldn't free agent memory" and says what went wrong. Before the 1.2.10 release it also did something else first. It ran xcrun simctl shutdown all, which shuts down every simulator on the Mac. The order was the bug. In both button handlers, the call that shuts down simulators sat above the check for whether Node.js had run. A person without Node.js would click the button, see "Nothing was changed", and have every running simulator shut down anyway. The receipt was false. Nothing in the app could have told them otherwise, because the shutdown happened before the app looked at the result. The change was moving one line below the check. items.title: MacOS widget that tells me which coding agents are waiting on me
items.summary: Agent Monitor: native desktop widgets for Claude Code and Codex. Usage limits at a glance, plus a live list of sessions stuck on approvals, questions or your next prompt. My usual afternoon looks like this: three or four Claude Code and Codex sessions running in parallel, in different projects, in different windows. One is refactoring an API, one is writing tests, one is fixing a landing page. And every twenty minutes I discover that one of them has been sitting there for a quarter of an hour, politely waiting for me to approve npm run deploy. Another one asked me a question and went idle. A third finished ages ago and I never noticed. The agents got fast. I became the bottleneck. So I built a small thing to fix that. Agent Monitor is a native macOS app with WidgetKit widgets and a menu bar icon. It answers two questions without me opening anything: Who is waiting on me, and why? How much of my usage limits is left? The Waiting on you list puts blockers first, in red: a tool call that needs approval, a question from the agent, a plan to review. items.title: Annoying Trump and dodging Flock: inside MapQuest’s contrarian comeback
items.summary: After refusing to obey the president’s Lake Ontario order, MapQuest briefly rose to No 1 in navigation apps. It’s now a tool in the US anti-surveillance movement I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech. Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs. Continue reading...

items.summary: NASA's Voyager 1 has become the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth, or 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). This means radio signals will take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft, now nearly 50 years into its mission. From the report: But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA. [...] At any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. items.title: I optimized my iOS app for the foldable iPhone before it ships
items.summary: Apple's foldable iPhone is coming, and I wanted my app to be ready on day one instead of scrambling after launch. I'm a solo indie developer, and yesterday I submitted a new build of Fambind, my family organization app for iOS, with a layout optimized for the foldable iPhone. It's in App Review now. A new screen shape is a rare chance to look good while most apps still look stretched or awkward. For a small indie app, being ready early is one of the few advantages I have over bigger teams. It also forced me to clean up assumptions I had been carrying around for years. No more hardcoded sizes. Anything that assumed "an iPhone is this wide" had to go. Adaptive layouts. Screens adjust to the space they get instead of assuming one fixed shape. Using the extra room well. On a bigger canvas, a family app can show more at once, like a shared calendar next to the details, without more taps. Testing in the simulator at different sizes, including the ones I hope are close to the real thing. If your layout only works on one screen size, you have a bug you haven't found yet. items.title: Inside swiftc: How Swift Turns Source into SIL, LLVM IR and Machine Code
items.summary: One small function followed through every stage of the Swift compiler, with real SIL, LLVM IR and x86-64 / ARM64 assembly, and a measured look at how optimization changes the cost of protocols, generics, closures and classes. Source → Lexer → Parser → AST → Type checker → SIL → SIL optimizer → LLVM IR → LLVM optimizer → Machine code → Object file → Linker → Binary Last year I lost most of an afternoon to a single line of arithmetic. It was in a geometry helper, nothing clever, a handful of numbers, a couple of Double(...) conversions and some parentheses. Every clean build took noticeably longer than it should have, and when I finally ran the compiler with type-checking timers switched on, that one line was the culprit. That sent me down a path I'd been avoiding for years: actually reading what swiftc produces between my source file and the binary. This article is the write-up I wish I'd had at the start. We'll follow one tiny function through every stage of the pipeline. We'll look at real SIL, real LLVM IR and real assembly. items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Hill: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) confirmed Tuesday that it was withdrawing the U.S.'s measles elimination status, ending more than two decades of what is considered to be one of the greatest public health achievements in modern history. The U.S. met with PAHO's Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission for a three-day, closed-door meeting last week. "The commission concluded that the endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn, a recommendation which I have accepted," Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO's director, said during the briefing Tuesday. The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000 and has held onto that for more than 25 years. But the past two years have seen close to 8,000 measles infections and roughly a dozen related deaths. This year has been the worst in terms of transmission in more than 30 years. items.title: Researchers track whole body movement with just a smartwatch (6 minute read)
items.summary: EchoMotion is a technology that can track the movement of a person's entire body using ultrasonic sound waves with just an off-the-shelf smartwatch and a lightweight AI model. items.title: US moves to cut China's remote access to AI chips (9 minute read)
items.summary: The US Commerce Department is closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals to bypass export restrictions on advanced computer chips by renting access to them from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. items.title: World 2030 (8 minute read)

items.title: The avalanche that hit math is coming for AI development (50 minute read)
items.summary: AI's capabilities in mathematics exploded quickly. Current AIs can now complete well-scoped problems in mathematics easily. items.title: Handing over humanity (22 minute read)
items.summary: Some AI experts believe that once we achieve superintelligence, humans will be permanently disempowered, and we shall all be ruled by an AI god. This might not be such a desirable outcome, as humans have a natural desire for freedom. The arrangement will probably not work, as keeping power responsive to human needs has required checks developed over centuries, sustained by repeated feedback from the real world and correction, and there's no reason to keep that equilibrium stable once humans have surrendered all control. Humans have the ability now to steer the technology in a way that will not lead to a complete replacement of human judgment.

The work is meant to separate filler-token reasoning from steganographic hidden reasoning when interpreting chain-of-thought.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.
